You are in an **Archon Horizon** workspace at `.`.

Load the **`horizon`** skill FIRST. Read it at the ABSOLUTE path
`/home/axel/LeanAlgebraicGeometry-Horizon/.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` (also exported as `$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`) — do NOT use a
relative path like `.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md`, which fails when your
shell starts in a member project rather than the workspace root. The skill
explains where the state lives, the tools, and this workspace's conventions
(one-shot discipline, git commits, the final report).

Before modifying files, inspect the required and conversational inbox lanes:
`"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --mine --status open --kind protection --json`
then `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --mine --unread --kind conversation --json`.
Protections are standing constraints even when already read. Address or explicitly
acknowledge unread conversations before ordinary advisory inbox material.

# Task
Task: ajcr-p3
Title: AJCR prover p3: claim and close the 3rd-most important representability item
Project(s) — work across all of them:
- Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild at MainProjects/Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild
References: roadmap=AJCR.jacobian,AJCR.w4-rep,AJCR.w4-rep.datum; inbox=I-0838

You are prover lane `ajcr-p3` on Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild. This round the objective is deliberately FREE: nobody has told you which declaration to prove. Your objective is to identify the THIRD most important open item standing between this project and Picard/Pic^0 representability, claim it publicly, and discharge it.

READ FIRST: protection item `I-0838`. It is the claim protocol for this round's ten parallel lanes and it is not optional — steps 2 through 5 (check ownership, claim with `roadmap set --owner ajcr-p3`, announce, release on exit) are what stop four lanes proving the same lemma. Also read `I-0491` and `I-0492`, the two binding human decisions, before touching the seam.

YOUR RANK. You take the THIRD most important item. Rank is a tie-break so four lanes do not converge on one target, not a fence: if your item turns out to be blocked on another lane's, say so in the inbox and swap. On a contested item you yield to p1 or p2, then take the next.

YOUR PEERS this round are ajcr-p1, ajcr-p2, ajcr-p3, ajcr-p4 plus the reviewer `review-ajcr`. The reviewer is auditing route and organisation and will be correcting the board in its first hour — read its inbox items before you fix your target, and re-read them if you are about to start something large. It may direct-message you a proposal; weigh it against what you hold, and take it if it is genuinely worth more. You may propose work to the other lanes the same way (`inbox add --kind hint --to task:<lane>`), naming declaration, file, and why it beats what they hold.

HOW TO CHOOSE, since this is the part I am delegating to you. "Most important" means: measured against the project's representability headline, what does discharging this buy? A leaf that unblocks three others beats a leaf that is merely nearest. A leaf whose stated prerequisite turns out to already exist in the file beats both — earlier sessions' costings in this workspace have been wrong in that direction more than once, so read the actual Lean hypothesis, not the prose about it. Use `horizon graph -p Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild frontier` for the ranked view, `horizon roadmap list --focus AJCR.w4-rep` for the board, and `horizon search` (which spans both projects AND mathlib) before you prove anything — the premise you need is often already next door under a name you would not have grepped.

THE BAR, and it is higher than usual this round. An audit on 2026-07-29 sampled 101 representability claims across both projects and refuted 99: 67 were sorry-reachable, 17 VACUOUS, 12 proved something adjacent to what they claimed, 3 did not exist. So:
- Sorry-free is necessary, not sufficient. Before you report a gate closed, exhibit a witness for EVERY antecedent, or state plainly which antecedent remains undischarged. "The implication is proved" and "the conclusion holds for some curve" are different claims and I want to know which you have.
- Never introduce a class, structure field, or side condition whose statement does not mention the object it is about. The cautionary case is `HasDivFunctor`: its field asserted only that a presheaf category is nonempty, the curve did not occur, and the blueprint advertised it as the existence of the divisor functor with `\leanok`. It survived because nobody read the statement.
- Never discharge an obligation by projecting the hypothesis you assumed. `choose_spec.1` of your own binder is `P → P`.
- A green build is not evidence of non-vacuity, and `lean_multi_attempt` reports every snippet as closing the goal when the file's imports are stale. Check imports before believing a probe.
- Do not restate an obligation more weakly to make a count go down. If you cannot close it, leave it open and say why.

ONE SHARED LEDGER, ten writers. Another lane's integrate sweep can commit your half-written file before you have measured it once — write risky proofs as explicit `sorry` first, measure, then fill. Stage explicit files, never `add -A`. Commit at every coherent point; an interrupted lane loses only what was uncommitted. Follow the `lean-check` LSP loop for edits and keep `lake build` for the session boundary — nine other lanes want the build lock too.

WHERE THIS PROJECT ACTUALLY STANDS, so you do not rediscover it. AJCR is the architecturally sound one. `pic0RepresentableByOfCharts` (`Picard/Pic0SigmaSheaf.lean:161`) and `mixedParamRepresentableBy` (`Picard/Pic0ChartAtlasParamFree.lean:125`) are genuinely sorry-free and kernel-confirmed on `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]` — honest, non-circular implications that WOULD produce a real representing scheme. The problem is that all three antecedents are undischarged, with no sorry-free witness for any: `IsChartUniv`, Zariski-local surjectivity of `Sigma.desc f`, and `rep i`. A correct machine with nothing to feed it.

That makes your choice unusually concrete: pick whichever of the three missing inputs you judge closest, or the leaf that most directly produces one. Do not treat the sorry count as the map — the 17 body sorries are 15 in `Challenge.lean` (the statement-only headline file, so those ARE the north star, not debt) and 2 in `Pic0ThetaCocycle.lean`. The real work is antecedents that no sorry marks.

The board under `AJCR.w4-rep` (51/74 done) has a deep tail worth reading with suspicion: under `datum.dat-d.ddr.certificate`, four siblings are `rejected` (`cert-relocalize`, `joint-cover`, `leak-image`, `tube-fibre`) and one is `blocked` (`away-kerspan`). Four rejections clustered under one parent usually means the parent's formulation is wrong, not that four different approaches each independently failed. The reviewer is determining which; read its finding before you spend a session inside that tail. Other open items to weigh: `datum.dat-b` (coverage + injectivity — every pic^0 point is hit), `datum.dat-c.c9-chartlocus` and its `chart-u` child (the co-signed chartLocus and its openness — the sole gate of dat-b B-6 AND the whole dat-glue), `datum.dat-d.ddr.divrep.u2` (the DDR9-U epsilon-identity at the universal point), `datum.dat-glue` (the 01JJ RepresentableBy assembly), `datum.dat-j`, `datum.dat-g`, `w4-rep.build-reach` (93 of 620 modules unrooted, so the axiom probe does not see them — a file nobody imports is a file nobody has measured, which may matter to whichever "sorry-free" claim you are relying on).

Costings in this project have been wrong before, in the expensive direction: a handoff demanded a new structure field where the localization lemma it asked for was already in the file. So for whatever leaf you pick, read its actual Lean hypothesis before accepting its stated price. An over-priced leaf is where you win this round.

The sibling project Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge is readable and `horizon search` spans both. It has more Quot/Serre machinery than this project does; if your leaf needs cohomological input, look there before building it. Price the consumer's carrier when you do — a cross-project match at object level can be true and irrelevant if the cover or instance your statement binds differs.

WHAT I WANT AT THE END. Your report should answer three things without me having to ask: which item you claimed and why it was the third-most important, what its state is now (closed sorry-free with all antecedents witnessed / closed as an implication with named antecedents still open / advanced with the remaining obligation stated / blocked, with the blocker), and what you learned that changes another lane's plan. If you found a costing wrong, a vacuity, or a route problem, that goes in the inbox as an `issue` at the site that made the claim — not only in your report, which nobody downstream reads.

If your first-choice item collapses on inspection — the prerequisite already exists, or the statement turns out vacuous, or another lane got there first — that is a finding, not a wasted session. Record it, release the claim, and take the next item. Do not sit on a claimed item you are not working.

This is a headless, one-shot session: advance the REAL objective, commit each
verified unit and any final edits, keep operational comments to the delta,
then write the skill's brief final report.

1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
60	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
61	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
62	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
63	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
64	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
65	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
66	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
67	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
68	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
69	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
70	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
71	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
72	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
73	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
74	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
75	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
76	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
77	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
78	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
79	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
80	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
81	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
82	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
83	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
84	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
85	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
86	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
87	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
88	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
89	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
90	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
91	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
92	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
93	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
94	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
95	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
96	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
97	
98	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
99	
100	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
101	
102	| Variable | Meaning |
103	|---|---|
104	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
105	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
112	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
113	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
114	
115	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
116	
117	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
118	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
119	
120	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
121	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
122	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
123	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
124	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
125	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
126	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
127	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
128	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
129	
130	## One-shot discipline (important)
131	
132	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
133	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
134	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
135	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
136	
137	## Pick the highest-value work
138	
139	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
140	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
141	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
142	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
143	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
144	
145	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
146	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
147	the objective is large. Leave a concise task comment only for a durable state
148	change or blocker, not every action. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
149	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
150	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
151	(it returns to the queue).
152	
153	## Fresh-context checkpoints
154	
155	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
156	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
157	checkpoints:
158	
159	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
160	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
161	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
162	  clean/build result.
163	
164	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
165	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
166	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
167	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
168	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
169	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
170	terminal `done` claim.
171	
172	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
173	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
174	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
175	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
176	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
177	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
178	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
179	
180	## Warnings are work
181	
182	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
183	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
184	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
185	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
186	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
187	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
188	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
189	why.
190	
191	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
192	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
193	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
194	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
195	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
196	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
197	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
198	
199	## Do the work (Lean)
200	
201	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
202	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
203	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
204	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
205	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
206	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
207	configured final build covers the same files.
208	
209	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
210	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
211	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
212	mathlib — query it:
213	
214	| You want | Use | Not |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
217	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
218	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
219	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
220	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
221	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
222	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
223	
224	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
225	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
226	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
227	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
228	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
229	back to grep.
230	
231	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
232	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
233	
234	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
235	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
236	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
237	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
238	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
239	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
240	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
241	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
242	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
243	
244	## Read the other projects
245	
246	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
247	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
248	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
249	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
250	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
251	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
252	
253	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
254	
255	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
256	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
257	needs no permission.
258	
259	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
260	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
261	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
262	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
263	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
264	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
265	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
266	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
267	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
268	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
269	
270	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
271	
272	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
273	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
274	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
275	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
276	
277	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
278	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
279	
280	- Commit after each independently useful verified proof, file, or bounded tooling
281	  change; commit before long builds/reviews and before expanding scope. Multi-hour
282	  implementation sessions normally produce several commits.
283	- Never end a session with durable authored changes after the last commit. The
284	  lifecycle hook gives a compact checkpoint reminder and may pause Stop when it
285	  observed a file mutation after the last commit.
286	- Keep operational prose as a delta. Task/roadmap/inbox comments default to one
287	  sentence or at most three bullets: conclusion, evidence, next action. Do not
288	  copy the report, commit summary, or thread history into them.
289	
290	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
291	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
292	  as **memory**.
293	
294	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
295	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
296	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
297	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
298	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
299	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
300	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
301	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
302	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
303	
304	## Resuming after an interruption
305	
306	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
307	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
308	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
309	
310	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
311	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
312	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
313	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
314	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
315	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
316	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
317	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
318	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
319	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
320	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
321	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
322	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
323	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
324	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
325	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
326	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
327	
328	## Final report (your last message)
329	
330	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
331	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
332	Use only sections that carry information: normally `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
333	`## Why I stopped`, and `## Next`. In `## Progress`, use one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
334	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
335	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
336	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
337	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
338	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
339	not by itself a reason to stop. Do not replay the chronological session log.
340	
341	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
342	
343	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
344	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
345	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
346	`subagents` skill):
347	
348	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
349	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
350	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
351	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
352	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
353	
354	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

8	/-!
9	# U2 as an equation between morphisms: the chart maps lie in the range of the classifier
10	
11	`Picard/DivRepAffPullClause.lean` reduced the whole divisor-representability chain to a
12	single hypothesis, `DivRepChartFamily.IsChartClause U`, and `IsChartClause.of_id` showed
13	that its `ω`-quantifier collapses to the identity point, i.e. to the DDR9-U ε-identity as
14	`informal/w4-ddr9-worksheet.md` §3.1 states it.  That is still a *submodule* identity with
15	a `∀`-quantifier over tower tests and framings hidden inside `IsDivRepClassify`.
16	
17	This file removes that quantifier.  The backward classifier `divRepClassifyZar`
18	(`Picard/DivRepClassifyZar.lean`) is defined for **every** locally certified class over
19	**every** affine test, unconditionally, and `isDivRepClassify_unique` says it is the
20	*only* morphism satisfying the clause.  So the clause is not an extra property at all:
21	
22	> `IsDivRepClassify F₀ v` ↔ `(divRepClassifyZar … F₀).left = v`.
23	
24	Both directions are one line — forward is uniqueness, backward is a rewrite — and the
25	consequence is that U2 becomes an **equation between two morphisms of schemes that both
26	already exist**:
27	
28	> U2 ↔ for each pair chart `(i, j)`, `(divRepClassifyZar … (U i j)).left = ChartMap i j`.
29	
30	Reading off the existential, the last obligation of divisor representability is that
31	each chart map lies in the **range** of the classifier at its own chart ring:
32	
33	> `divFunctor_representableBy_of_chartRange` :
34	>   `(∀ i j, ∃ F, (divRepClassifyZar … F).left = ChartMap i j) →`
35	>   `(divFunctor C π g).RepresentableBy DivOver`
36	
37	Since `divRepClassifyZar` is injective on classes (`eq_of_isDivRepClassify`,
38	`Picard/DivRepClassifyZarSep.lean`), representability of `divFunctor` is *equivalent* to
39	surjectivity of `divRepClassifyZar` at every affine test; what this file records is that
40	surjectivity at the **chart rings alone** suffices.  That is the honest content: the
41	classifier is already a bijection onto its range everywhere, and the whole remaining debt
42	is that the finitely many chart points are hit.
43	
44	## Main declarations
45	
46	* `AlgebraicGeometry.isDivRepClassify_iff_divRepClassifyZar_left_eq` — the clause **is**
47	  the classifier equation, in both directions.  General: no chart family, no universal
48	  point.
49	* `AlgebraicGeometry.DivRepChartFamily.isChartClause_iff_forall_classify_eq` — U2 as a
50	  per-chart equation of morphisms, **as an iff**, so it is a reduction and not merely a
51	  restatement (the safeguard of inbox `I-0571`).
52	* `AlgebraicGeometry.divFunctor_representableBy_of_chartRange` — divisor
53	  representability from range membership of the chart maps.
54	
55	## What this does NOT do
56	
57	It produces no class over a chart ring, so it clears no gate: U2 is unproved and, per
58	roadmap `…divrep.u2`, the production of a chart class with the tautological ε remains the
59	G-4 obligation.  What changes is what a producer has to exhibit — a class whose classifier
60	*is* the chart map, rather than a family satisfying a quantified submodule identity.  The
61	endpoint also still carries `hO`, `hχ` and the ambient curve instances.
62	-/

So a lane that can discharge CHART-U(c) *at one parameter* can discharge it index-by-index at
different parameters, with no additional compatibility between them — there is no coherence
condition across indices, because `pic0RepresentableByOfCharts` imposes none. -/
theorem isOpenImmersion_presheaf_mixedParamChart {ι : Type u} (nn : ι → ℕ)
    (D : ι → Over (Spec (.of k)))
    (rep : ∀ i, (divFunctor C π (nn i)).RepresentableBy (D i))
    (m : ι → ℕ) (Z : ι → (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : ∀ i, Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k (Z i)
      = (m i : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (nn i : ℤ))
    (V : ∀ i, (D i).left.Opens)
    (huniv : ∀ i, IsChartUniv C π (nn i) (rep i) (m i) (Z i) (hdeg i) (V i)) (i : ι) :
    IsOpenImmersion.presheaf (mixedParamChart C π nn D rep m Z hdeg V i) :=
  huniv i

variable (C π) in
/-- **A mixed-parameter chart family is admissible input to the DAT-glue seam.**

`pic0RepresentableByOfCharts` accepts it verbatim.  This is the statement that settles the
question `Pic0ChartCoverageIndexSlack` and I-0660 both left implicit: the representability engine
never sees a chart parameter, so the forced calibration `b = n` is a *per-chart* condition and
carries no uniformity obligation.

Note what remains hypothetical here and is not weakened by this: `hf` (i.e. `IsChartUniv`, still
CERT-Σ-gated), local surjectivity (DAT-B B-6), and the *existence* of `rep i` at parameters other
than `g` — which is the question this observation hands to the divisor-representability lane. -/
def mixedParamRepresentableBy {ι : Type u} (nn : ι → ℕ)
    (D : ι → Over (Spec (.of k)))
    (rep : ∀ i, (divFunctor C π (nn i)).RepresentableBy (D i))
    (m : ι → ℕ) (Z : ι → (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : ∀ i, Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k (Z i)
      = (m i : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (nn i : ℤ))
    (V : ∀ i, (D i).left.Opens)
    (hf : ∀ i, IsOpenImmersion.presheaf (mixedParamChart C π nn D rep m Z hdeg V i))
    [Presheaf.IsLocallySurjective Scheme.zariskiTopology
      (Sigma.desc (mixedParamChart C π nn D rep m Z hdeg V))] :
    (pic0TypeFunctor C).RepresentableBy
      (Over.mk ((Scheme.LocalRepresentability.representableBy hf).homEquiv
        (𝟙 (Scheme.LocalRepresentability.glueData hf).glued)).1) :=
  pic0RepresentableByOfCharts C (mixedParamChart C π nn D rep m Z hdeg V) hf

end

end AlgebraicGeometry

/-!
# THE ATLAS IS CHART-PARAMETER HETEROGENEOUS — each chart may carry its own `n`

`Picard/Pic0ChartCoverageIndexSlack.lean` establishes that at a chart index legal at parameter
`n` the coverage theorem's threshold is forced to equal `n`, and that at `n = g` the resulting
hypothesis is false.  Both that file and the review it adjudicates (I-0660) then reason about
"the" chart parameter, as though the atlas had one.

**It does not, and this file proves it.**  `pic0RepresentableByOfCharts`
(`Picard/Pic0SigmaSheaf.lean:161`) takes a family `f : ∀ i, yoneda.obj (X i) ⟶ pic0SigmaSheaf`
indexed by an arbitrary `ι`, with `X : ι → Scheme` and a *per-index* certificate
`hf : ∀ i, IsOpenImmersion.presheaf (f i)`.  Nothing ties the `X i` together, so nothing ties
their chart parameters together either: `mixedParamChart` below builds such a family from a
per-index parameter `nn : ι → ℕ`, a per-index representation of `divFunctor C π (nn i)`, and a
per-index chart index legal *at that index's own parameter*.

## Why this matters, and it changes the shape of the residue

The `b = n` calibration is per-chart.  So the question "can coverage use DAT-0a's threshold?"
does not have to be answered uniformly: a point whose splitting field has threshold `b_L` can be
covered by *the chart whose parameter is `b_L.toNat`*, and a different point by a different
chart.  The I-0204 non-uniformity of `m` — no single exponent works for every fibre — is
therefore **not** an obstruction to the atlas; it is an argument for an atlas indexed by the
threshold, which is what a heterogeneous family is.

What this does **not** do, and the honest limit of the observation:

* it does not produce the representations.  `mixedParamChart` takes `rep i` as a hypothesis, one
  per parameter, and the divisor-representability lane supplies `divFunctor C π g` — a single

/-- **The Abel transformation into the degree-zero Picard functor**: under the chart-index
degree constraint `deg Z = m·d₁ − n`, the chart value of `DivSchemeAbel.lean` — the Abel class
of the divisor family, shifted by the Σ-family of `Z` and by `m` inverse powers of the pinned
θ-family — is a natural transformation `divFunctor C π n ⟶ pic0TypeFunctor C`.

The degree ledger of `degAt_chartValue` is what makes the target the degree-*zero* functor:
the three factors contribute `n`, `deg Z` and `−m·d₁`, which the constraint sums to zero. -/
def chartValueTrans (m : ℕ) (Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k Z
      = (m : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (n : ℤ)) :
    divFunctor C π n ⟶ pic0TypeFunctor C where
  app T := TypeCat.ofHom fun s => ⟨chartValue C π n m Z T.unop s,
    chartValue_mem_pic0Subgroup C π n m Z hdeg T.unop s⟩
  naturality T T' g := by
    refine ConcreteCategory.hom_ext _ _ fun s => ?_
    exact Subtype.ext ((picEtMap_chartValue C π n m Z g.unop s).symm)

@[simp]
lemma chartValueTrans_app_coe (m : ℕ) (Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k Z
      = (m : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (n : ℤ))
    (T : (Over (Spec (.of k)))ᵒᵖ) (s : divFamZar C π n T.unop) :
    ((chartValueTrans C π n m Z hdeg).app T s).1 = chartValue C π n m Z T.unop s :=
  rfl

/-! ## The Abel chart map -/

variable (C π n) in
/-- **The Abel chart map** of a representation of the divisor functor: the morphism of big-site
presheaves `yoneda.obj D.left ⟶ pic0SigmaFunctor C` sending a `D`-point to the degree-zero class
of the divisor family that point names.

`rep` is a *hypothesis* — this file never constructs a representation of the divisor functor;
that is the divisor-representability obligation of the `DivRep…` lane.  Given one, this is the
Abel–Jacobi map at the level of the Σ-extension, and it is the only kind of object
`JacobianData.ofCharts` accepts. -/
def abelSigmaChart {D : Over (Spec (.of k))} (rep : (divFunctor C π n).RepresentableBy D)
    (m : ℕ) (Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k Z
      = (m : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (n : ℤ)) :
    yoneda.obj D.left ⟶ (pic0SigmaSheaf C).1 :=
  rep.toSigmaExtension ≫ Over.sigmaExtensionNat (chartValueTrans C π n m Z hdeg)

/-- **The structure morphism of the Abel chart is that of the representing object**: for the
one-element family consisting of the Abel chart map, the chart structure morphism `chartHom`
that `JacobianData.ofCharts` reads off is `D.hom` itself.

So the finiteness hypotheses of the producer, specialised to this chart, are exactly
`LocallyOfFiniteType D.hom` and `CompactSpace D.left` — properties of the divisor scheme, with
no reference to the Picard functor. -/
lemma chartHom_abelSigmaChart {D : Over (Spec (.of k))}
    (rep : (divFunctor C π n).RepresentableBy D)
    (m : ℕ) (Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
    (hdeg : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg k Z
      = (m : ℤ) * classDeg k (thetaCechClass C) - (n : ℤ))
    {ι : Type u} (i : ι) :
    chartHom C (fun _ : ι => abelSigmaChart C π n rep m Z hdeg) i = D.hom :=
  Category.id_comp _

end
